Headline: The situation in 1763–4
Text:
• Boston’s natural harbour supported shipping, shipbuilding, cod fishing and the rum trade.
  • New England merchants often used molasses from the French Caribbean, despite British trade restrictions.
  • Earlier molasses duties encouraged smuggling and did not reliably increase British revenue.
  • The Seven Years’ War left Britain with heavy debts and the cost of defending a larger empire.
  • British decisions increasingly came from London, while colonists had little direct influence over Parliament.
Media Caption: A 1775 chart of Boston Harbor, the port at the centre of the imperial dispute. Source record: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:A_plan_of_the_town_and_chart_of_the_harbour_of_Boston_-_exhibiting_a_view_of_the_islands,_castle_forts,_and_entrances_into_the_said_harbour._LOC_2001624924.jpg
Alt Text: Historic map of Boston town and harbour, published in 1775.

Headline: Pontiac’s rebellion 1763
Text:
• Britain’s victory in the Seven Years’ War removed France as the main imperial rival in much of North America.
  • Pontiac’s rebellion showed that British control of newly acquired territories remained uncertain.
  • Britain kept troops in America to defend its territories and maintain order.
  • Ministers argued that the colonies should help pay for the cost of defence.

Headline: Sugar Act 1764
Text:
• The Sugar Act changed duties on molasses and strengthened customs enforcement against smuggling.
  • Molasses was important to New England’s rum trade, so merchants feared higher costs and stricter controls.
  • Colonists objected to revenue measures imposed by a Parliament in which they had no elected representatives.

Headline: Americans should pay
Text:
• Prime Minister George Grenville argued that the colonies should contribute to imperial defence and administration.
  • Britain faced heavy debts after the Seven Years’ War and the expense of maintaining troops overseas.
  • British officials wanted taxes collected more effectively and smuggling reduced.
  • Many colonists accepted the need for defence but disputed Parliament’s right to tax them without representation.

Headline: The Stamp Act 1765
Text:
• The Stamp Act required paid stamps on printed materials, including newspapers and legal documents.
  • Publishers, printers, lawyers and people using official documents were directly affected.
  • Because it taxed items used within the colonies, opposition spread through newspapers, petitions and public meetings.
  • Colonists argued that taxation without their own elected representatives was unjust.
Media Caption: An extract from the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed printed materials and legal documents. Source record: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:1765_Stamp_Act.jpg
Alt Text: Printed extract from the British Stamp Act of 1765.

Headline: American opposition
Text:
• “No taxation without representation” became a central protest slogan.
  • Colonial assemblies passed resolutions and pamphlets spread arguments against the Stamp Act.
  • Crowds used demonstrations and effigies to intimidate tax officials.
  • Andrew Oliver, appointed to administer the stamp tax in Massachusetts, faced protests and resigned.
  • The Sons of Liberty helped organise resistance, although some protests involved threats and property damage.

Headline: Repeal of Stamp Act 1766
Text:
• Parliament repealed the Stamp Act in 1766 after colonial resistance and pressure from British merchants worried about lost trade.
  • Many colonists celebrated the repeal as a victory for their protests.
  • The Declaratory Act stated that Parliament could legislate for the colonies “in all cases whatsoever”.
  • The immediate crisis eased, but the disagreement over Parliament’s authority remained.
Media Caption: The political cartoon “The Triumph of America” appeared in London newspapers in 1766, amid the Stamp Act controversy and its repeal. Source record: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Stamp_Act_1765_-_Triumph_of_America.jpg
Alt Text: Eighteenth-century political cartoon titled The Triumph of America.

Headline: Townshend duties 1767
Text:
• The Townshend duties placed import taxes on goods including glass, lead, paint, paper and tea.
  • Customs enforcement increased, and colonial merchants organised boycotts and non-importation agreements.
  • Officials sought military support as resistance grew.
  • Two British regiments arrived in Boston in 1768; many residents viewed their presence as an occupation rather than protection.

Headline: American opposition
Text:
• Colonial assemblies circulated the Circular Letters to encourage joint opposition to the Townshend duties.
  • Popular protests and the Sons of Liberty kept resistance visible.
  • Merchants used economic sanctions and non-importation agreements to pressure Britain.
  • The arrival of British troops in Boston increased tension between soldiers and local residents.

Headline: Boston Massacre 1770
Text:
• On 5 March 1770, a crowd confronted British soldiers in Boston.
  • Soldiers fired into the crowd, killing five colonists, including Crispus Attucks.
  • Patriot leaders used the deaths to argue that standing armies threatened colonial liberty.
  • The confrontation involved fear, provocation and confusion; it was not simply an unprovoked attack in the way some propaganda suggested.
Media Caption: Paul Revere’s influential 1770 engraving portrayed the Boston Massacre and helped shape colonial opinion. It is a contemporary political image, not a neutral photograph of the event. Source record: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_bloody_massacre_by_Paul_Revere.jpg
Alt Text: Paul Revere’s hand-coloured engraving depicting the Boston Massacre in 1770.

Headline: Repeal of Townshend duties 1770
Text:
• Britain repealed most Townshend duties in 1770 to reduce tensions and protect trade.
  • The duty on tea remained.
  • Keeping the tea duty was partly symbolic: Parliament wanted to maintain its claimed right to tax the colonies.
  • The dispute therefore continued even though most of the duties had been removed.

Headline: Calm (1770–3)
Text:
• Tensions eased after most Townshend duties were repealed.
  • Many colonists returned to everyday life, and large-scale confrontation became less frequent.
  • The tea duty remained, so the underlying dispute over Parliament’s authority was unresolved.
  • The period was a pause in the crisis, not a lasting settlement.

Headline: 1773 Tea Act
Text:
• The Tea Act allowed the East India Company (EIC) to ship tea directly to the colonies, cutting out British middlemen.
  • The EIC was in serious financial difficulty and owed large sums; Parliament wanted to prevent its collapse.
  • Class notes also link the crisis to the devastating Bengal famine, in which over one million people died.
  • The tea could be cheaper than smuggled tea, but the existing tax remained.
  • Many colonists feared buying it would accept Parliament’s right to tax them.
Media Caption: Portrait of Benjamin Franklin, the colonial writer, scientist and diplomat who moved between British and American political circles. Source record: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Benjamin_Franklin_Portrait.jpg

Headline: The Boston Tea Party 1773
Text:
• Tea ships reached Boston in late 1773. Merchants had a limited time to unload the cargo and pay the duty.
  • Governor Thomas Hutchinson insisted that the tea be landed, while town meetings demanded that it leave without the tax being paid.
  • Meetings moved from Faneuil Hall to the larger Old South Meeting House, attracting thousands.
  • On 16 December, after debate and Samuel Adams’s final remarks, people boarded the ships and dumped the EIC tea into Boston Harbor.
  • Participants damaged the tea but took care not to destroy other property; a broken lock was reportedly returned to its owner.
  • The protest was organised and deliberate, although participants included people from different backgrounds.
Media Caption: A later historical illustration of the Boston Tea Party, when protestors destroyed East India Company tea in Boston Harbor on 16 December 1773. Source record: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Boston_tea_party.jpg
Alt Text: Historical illustration of the Boston Tea Party in Boston Harbor.

Headline: The Coercive Acts 1774
Text:
• News of the Boston Tea Party reached Britain in January 1774 and provoked outrage.
  • Parliament passed the Coercive Acts, called the Intolerable Acts by many colonists, to punish Massachusetts and restore British authority.
  • The measures closed Boston’s port until the tea was paid for and restricted local self-government.
  • Rather than isolating Boston, the punishment encouraged other colonies to support Massachusetts.
Media Caption: A 1775 map of Boston and the surrounding countryside, showing the road to Concord and the geography behind Britain’s efforts to reassert control. Source record: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:A_plan_of_the_town_and_harbour_of_Boston_and_the_country_adjacent_with_the_road_from_Boston_to_Concord,_shewing_the_place_of_the_late_engagement_between_the_King%27s_troops_%26_the_provincials,_together_LOC_gm71002447.jpg
Alt Text: Historic map of Boston, its harbour and the road toward Concord.

Headline: The Québec Act
Text:
• The Québec Act reorganised government in Quebec and extended its boundaries into territory claimed by some mainland colonies.
  • It was not itself one of the punitive Coercive Acts, but colonists often viewed it alongside them.
  • Together, the measures strengthened fears that Britain was expanding its power without colonial consent.

Headline: The American response
Text:
• Colonies responded to the Coercive Acts with political cooperation and economic sanctions.
  • Boycotts and non-importation agreements aimed to pressure British merchants and the government.
  • Many colonists saw the punishment of Massachusetts as a threat to the rights of every colony.
  • The dispute was becoming an intercolonial crisis rather than only a conflict between Britain and Boston.

Headline: Political actions
Text:
• Colonists organised extra-legal conventions and local Committees of Safety to coordinate resistance.
  • The First Continental Congress met in Philadelphia in September 1774.
  • Delegates coordinated a response to the Coercive Acts, supported Massachusetts and petitioned against British policies.
  • These organisations helped colonies cooperate beyond local assemblies and prepared them for further resistance.
Media Caption: A coloured rendition of Henry Samuel Sadd’s painting depicting prayer at the First Continental Congress, which met in Philadelphia in 1774. Source record: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:1st-continental-congress-1.jpg
Alt Text: Painting depicting delegates at the First Continental Congress.

Headline: British determination
Text:
• British leaders wanted to restore royal authority and were unwilling to accept continued resistance.
  • General Thomas Gage, also governor of Massachusetts, was responsible for British troops in the colony.
  • British authorities planned to seize colonial military supplies around Concord.
  • The attempt to enforce British policy brought the political crisis to the point of armed conflict.

Headline: Lexington and Concord 1775
Text:
• On 19 April 1775, British regulars and colonial militia clashed at Lexington.
  • Fighting continued at Concord as British troops searched for military supplies.
  • Militia members attacked British troops during their retreat toward Boston.
  • The battles marked the shift from protest and political resistance to open warfare.
Media Caption: A stylised historical engraving of the Battle of Lexington; it is an artistic depiction rather than a precise eyewitness record. Source record: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Battle_of_Lexington,_1775.png
Alt Text: Stylised engraving depicting the Battle of Lexington, 19 April 1775.

Headline: War 1775
Text:
• Fighting at Lexington and Concord in April 1775 began the American Revolutionary War.
  • The conflict had grown from disputes over imperial debts and taxation into a struggle over representation and political authority.
  • The use of British troops deepened the crisis and made reconciliation harder.
  • The Second Continental Congress later organised the colonial war effort.
